elements.texte:
[cheerful] Every Monday, management checks a website dashboard.

It tracks three indicators there: the number of customers, of orders and of products.

We count the rows of three tables: the customers table, the orders table and the products table.

Management wants to bring these three indicators together in a single result to feed its dashboard.
elements.avant: Combine the results of several queries one after the other.
elements.apres: One by one, these indicators come from a count star on each table.
phrases: Every Monday, management checks a website dashboard.
It tracks three indicators there: the number of customers, of orders and of products.
We count the rows of three tables: the customers table, the orders table and the products table.
Management wants to bring these three indicators together in a single result to feed its dashboard.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] One by one, these indicators come from a count star on each table.

But that makes three queries, and three separate results.

A join doesn’t fit: there’s no row to link here.

We need to stack the three rows, one under the other.
elements.avant: Management wants to bring these three indicators together in a single result to feed its dashboard.
elements.apres: UNION ALL combines the rows of several select queries into a single result, keeping the duplicates.
phrases: One by one, these indicators come from a count star on each table.
But that makes three queries, and three separate results.

We need to stack the three rows, one under the other.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] UNION ALL combines the rows of several select queries into a single result, keeping the duplicates.

Here, each select returns one indicator: so we get three rows, one per indicator.

We get a single result, with three rows and one column: 10 customers, 16 orders and 8 products.

Each row contains the value of one indicator.

UNION would leave out duplicate rows, whereas UNION ALL keeps them all.

UNION ALL is therefore the right choice: with UNION, two equal indicators would make a single row.

The three indicators are brought together, but nothing says what they stand for.

There’s a label missing to tell apart the customers, the orders and the products.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] To say what each indicator stands for, we add a label in each select:

Number of customers, Number of orders or Number of products.

It appears next to the matching value.

The first select sets the names of the result’s columns:

Indicator for the labels and value for the results of the count star queries, thanks to the aliases written with as.

These aliases only need to be defined in the first select.

The following select queries add their values to the same columns:

The label first, the indicator second.

Each select now returns two columns, in the same order:

The indicator’s label, then the matching indicator.

UNION ALL brings these rows together in a single result.

[cheerful] Careful: you received an email about a new additional need:

Management would also like to track the number in stock.

Added as a third column, it makes the query impossible to run.

Two columns at the top, three at the bottom: the rows can’t be stacked.

For one more indicator, you need one more row, with its two columns.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] The complete query stacks the four select queries with UNION ALL, including the one for the number in stock.

Result: 4 rows, each with the indicator’s name and its value.

The dashboard shows 10 customers, 16 orders, 8 products and 1,075 units in stock.

To remember it: join widens the result, UNION lengthens it.
